item.title: Biwako Valley: Ropeway, Sky Views and Winter Slopes — Guide
item.description: Biwako Valley, on the Hira mountains above Otsu, is Shiga’s easiest mountain thrill: a ropeway climbs some 1,100 metres in about five minutes to a summit plateau with one of the finest panoramas in the Kansai region — the whole silver expanse of Lake Biwa spread out below. In the green season the draw is the cliff-edge ‘Biwako Terrace’, a café-lounge with infinity-style decks that seem to float over the lake, plus ziplines and treetop adventure courses; in winter the same slopes become a ski and snowboard resort within an hour of Kyoto, making it a rare day-trip peak for city-based visitors.

item.title: Kunozan Toshogu: The Original Resting Place of Tokugawa Ieyasu — Guide
item.description: Kunozan Toshogu is the original shrine of Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, built on Mount Kuno overlooking Suruga Bay immediately after his death in 1616 as his first burial place, before his remains were later enshrined at the more famous Nikko. Its brilliantly ornate halls, decorated with lacquer, gold leaf and intricate carvings, are designated National Treasures and predate Nikko’s, and the shrine is reached either by a scenic ropeway from the Nihondaira plateau or by climbing more than 1,100 stone steps up from the coast below.

item.title: Gifu Castle: A Mountaintop Castle With Sweeping Valley Views — Guide
item.description: Gifu Castle sits dramatically atop 329-metre Mount Kinka, reached by a ropeway followed by a short walk, and was once the stronghold of the warlord Oda Nobunaga, who launched his campaign to unify Japan from here in the 16th century. Though the current keep is a modern reconstruction, its commanding hilltop position offers sweeping panoramic views over Gifu City, the Nagara River winding below and the surrounding plains, making the journey up as much about the vista as the castle itself.

item.title: Nasu Highlands & Mount Chausu: A Volcanic Resort Above the Clouds — Guide
item.description: The Nasu Highlands, centred on the active volcanic peak of Mount Chausu (1,915 m), have been a favoured cool-climate retreat since the imperial family established a summer villa here in the early 20th century. A ropeway carries visitors partway up the still-steaming volcano for panoramic views and hiking trails across the crater rim, while the surrounding highland resort area hosts a changing calendar of seasonal events, from spring flower festivals to summer outdoor concerts and autumn foliage celebrations.

item.title: Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route: Cross the Japan Alps by Cable Car & Ropeway — Guide
item.description: The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route is a spectacular mountain-crossing transport route through the Northern Japan Alps, linking Toyama and Nagano prefectures via a chain of cable cars, ropeways, a trolleybus and highland buses that together climb over 2,400 metres above sea level. The route passes dramatic alpine scenery, including the famous Snow Corridor walls, and in winter and spring the surrounding slopes around Murodo also offer skiing and snowboarding for visitors wanting to combine alpine transport with time on the mountain itself.

item.title: Zao Snow Monsters (Juhyo): Miyagi's Frost Giants — Guide
item.description: Zao’s ‘snow monsters’ (juhyo) are one of Japan’s most surreal natural phenomena — fir trees on the Zao plateau above 1,400 m are encased in successive layers of freezing fog and blizzard snow from January through February, creating enormous white figures that fill the ski slopes like a silent army of frost giants. The Zao resort straddles the Miyagi-Yamagata border; the Miyagi side is less crowded and offers equally spectacular juhyo fields, best viewed from the ropeway gondola at dawn.

item.title: Hakkoda Mountains: Snow Monsters, Ropeway & Skiing — Guide
item.description: The Hakkoda Mountains, a volcanic range 20 minutes from Aomori City, see some of Japan’s deepest snow. The year-round ropeway climbs to 1,324 m: summer brings alpine flowers and panoramas, while winter creates the famous ‘snow monsters’ (juhyo) and world-class powder skiing. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City area, Aomori Hours Ropeway ~9:00–16:20 Admission Ropeway ~¥1,900 (round trip) Time needed 2–3 hours Best time Summer (alpine); Jan–Mar (snow monsters) What to See The ropeway to 1,324 m with 360-degree views.

item.title: Mt. Moriyoshi: Akita's Snow Monsters & Ropeway — Guide
item.description: Mt. Moriyoshi (1,454 m) in Kitaakita is a gentle peak reached by ropeway, famed for two very different seasons — winter ‘snow monsters’ (juhyo), fir trees encased in wind-sculpted rime ice, and summer carpets of alpine flowers across the highland. The ropeway makes both spectacles accessible without a hard climb. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kitaakita, Akita Hours Ropeway seasonal (winter & green season) Admission Ropeway fee applies Time needed 2–3 hours Best time Feb (snow monsters); summer flowers What to See Winter ‘snow monsters’ (juhyo) of rime-encased firs.

item.title: Hakone Guide: Mt. Fuji Views, Ropeway & Lake Ashi
item.description: Hakone is the Tokyo area’s favourite mountain getaway — a volcanic resort region of hot springs, lakes and, on clear days, postcard views of Mt. Fuji. The classic experience is the “Hakone loop,” a fun chain of scenic transport: a switchback mountain railway, a cable car, the Hakone Ropeway soaring over the steaming Owakudani valley, and a pirate-ship cruise across Lake Ashi, where Fuji rises beyond a lakeside torii gate. Add world-class onsen, art museums and easy access from Tokyo, and Hakone is one of Japan’s most rewarding day trips or overnight escapes.

item.title: Tokushima Leisure Guide: Rafting, Rope Cars & Awa Puppet Theater
item.description: Tokushima Prefecture occupies the eastern portion of Shikoku, Japan’s smallest main island, and it rewards visitors who slow down and engage with its landscape on its own terms. The Yoshino River — one of Japan’s three great rapids rivers — cuts through mountains that drop sharply from ridgelines nearly 2,000 metres above sea level. Narrow vine bridges span chasms in valleys where sunlight reaches the forest floor for only a few hours each day.
